mcqs.question: A button looks visually large with generous padding, but users on real devices frequently miss it when tapping. What's the most likely cause?
options: The button's color contrast is too low to see clearly
The button is placed in an unreachable area of the screen
The visible padding is decorative and not included in the actual hit-testing bounds, so the tappable area is smaller than the minimum recommended touch target size
The device's touchscreen sensitivity is set too low
mcqs.explanation: The recommended minimum touch target sizes apply to the actual hit-testing region, not the visual appearance — padding that's purely decorative and excluded from hit-testing leaves a target that looks fine but is genuinely too small to reliably hit with a thumb.

mcqs.question: A core action (deleting an important item) is only accessible via a swipe gesture, with no visible button or menu alternative. What's the main risk?
options: Gestures always perform worse than buttons in terms of raw speed
The gesture has no discoverability for first-time users and is effectively invisible to screen reader users unless an equivalent labelled action is explicitly exposed
Gestures cannot be implemented consistently across Android and iOS
Swipe gestures always conflict with system-level edge gestures
mcqs.explanation: A gesture with no visible affordance is easy for a first-time user to simply never discover, and it's invisible entirely to a screen reader user unless a labelled alternative action is deliberately exposed — the safe pattern for a core action is a gesture plus a discoverable equivalent, never a gesture alone.

mcqs.question: A custom-drawn slider control works perfectly for sighted users but is completely unusable with TalkBack or VoiceOver enabled. What's the most likely reason?
options: Screen readers are fundamentally incompatible with any custom-drawn UI
The control lacks the accessibility label, role, and state metadata that platform accessibility APIs need — standard widgets get this for free, but custom-drawn controls need it attached explicitly
The device needs a firmware update to support custom controls
TalkBack and VoiceOver only work with text-based interfaces
mcqs.explanation: Standard platform widgets expose accessibility metadata automatically, but a custom-drawn control has no such metadata unless the developer explicitly attaches a label, role, and state — without it, a screen reader has nothing to announce or act on, making the control effectively invisible to that interaction model.

mcqs.question: An app requests camera, location, contacts, and microphone permissions all at once during first-launch onboarding, before any feature needing them is used. What's the likely outcome?
options: Higher overall grant rates, since the user only has to respond to one screen instead of several

Users are likely to deny some or all of these out of context, and those denials are often effectively permanent without a manual settings visit — a lower opt-in rate than asking in context when each feature is actually used
This has no effect on grant rates since users always read permission prompts carefully
The OS blocks batched permission requests automatically
mcqs.explanation: Requesting sensitive permissions with no context for why they're needed reliably produces worse opt-in than asking right when a specific feature needs it, and because a denial is often hard to reverse without the user visiting settings, an out-of-context batch request can permanently cost you a permission a user would have happily granted later with proper context.

mcqs.question: A developer tests a button's tap target using a mouse cursor in an emulator and finds no issue, but real users on physical devices report missed taps. Why does the emulator test miss the bug?
options: A mouse cursor is a precise pixel-point input that trivially lands exactly where aimed, unlike a thumb, which covers a much coarser patch of screen and lands imprecisely, especially in motion
Emulators do not render touch targets at the correct size
The bug only exists on Android devices, and the emulator was running iOS
Real devices apply different touch target minimums than emulators
mcqs.explanation: A mouse in an emulator hits a target with pixel precision every time, which can never reproduce the coarser, less precise contact area of a real thumb — this is exactly why testing on a physical device with an actual finger is necessary to catch hit-area bugs that emulator testing structurally cannot surface.

mcqs.question: A delete button's accessibility label is set to "trash icon" rather than describing what tapping it does. Why does this fail a screen reader user even though a label technically exists?
options: The label is too short to be read aloud by the screen reader
Icon-based labels are never supported by any screen reader
A screen reader user needs to know what activating the control does, not what the picture looks like — a label describing the icon rather than the action leaves the actual function unclear
The label should instead be the exact filename of the icon asset for consistency
mcqs.explanation: Passing an audit checklist by having any label at all misses the point — a screen reader user needs the label to answer "what happens if I activate this," so describing the visual ("trash icon") instead of the action ("Delete item") leaves the actual function ambiguous or wrong.
